title: Trump Administration Appeals H-1B Fee Ruling as $100,000 Charge Stays in Effect Pending Court Decision
excerpt: The government argues the fee is not a tax and falls within presidential authority, while the First Circuit weighs whether to keep the fee alive during the appeal.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A federal judge ruled the $100,000 H-1B fee an unlawful tax but stayed the ruling pending appeal.
  • The Department of Homeland Security argues the fee is within presidential authority and not a tax.
  • USCIS continues to collect the $100,000 fee on H-1B petitions during the appeal process.
  • Multiple lawsuits challenging the fee are ongoing in federal courts across the U.S.
  • The fee significantly escalates H-1B filing costs, impacting Indian IT professionals and employers.
  • A federal judge struck down the $100,000 H-1B visa fee as an unlawful tax on June 8, but stayed the ruling on June 12 pending appeal
  • The Department of Homeland Security filed its appeal to the First Circuit, arguing the fee falls within presidential immigration authority
  • USCIS continues to collect the $100,000 fee on qualifying H-1B petitions while the appeal proceeds
  • Multiple lawsuits challenging the fee remain pending in federal courts across the country

The $100,000 H-1B visa fee that has shaken the Indian tech workforce remains in effect as the Trump administration presses its appeal of a federal court ruling that declared it an unconstitutional tax — a legal battle that will determine the cost of sponsoring skilled foreign workers in the United States for years to come.

What Happened

On June 8, 2026, Judge Leo Sorokin of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the $100,000 fee in its entirety, ruling that President Trump lacked the authority to impose what the court called an unlawful tax on H-1B petitions. The fee had been established through a September 2025 presidential proclamation and applied to new H-1B petitions requiring consular processing.

But the relief was short-lived. Just four days later, on June 12, the government filed a notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, and Judge Sorokin agreed to temporarily stay his own ruling. The practical effect: USCIS may continue collecting the $100,000 fee while the appeal moves forward.

The Government's Argument

In its filing to the First Circuit, the Department of Homeland Security argued that the fee is not properly considered a tax and that the president has broad authority under federal immigration law to impose it. "Every day that passes more aliens can petition and enter the country despite the President's determination that their entry would be detrimental," the government wrote, according to Bloomberg Tax.

"The President had no power or delegated authority to impose a tax on H-1B petitions."

— Judge Leo Sorokin, U.S. District Court for Massachusetts

The government also warned that even if it prevails on appeal, it would be difficult to revoke visas already issued and remove workers who entered without paying the fee.

What This Means for Indian Professionals

The $100,000 fee represented a dramatic escalation from the customary H-1B filing costs of $1,700 to $4,500. For Indian IT professionals and their employers — who account for the vast majority of H-1B petitions — the fee has effectively frozen new sponsorship plans and pushed companies to explore alternatives.

Immigration attorneys say employers should anticipate that USCIS will continue enforcing the fee requirement unless and until a court orders otherwise. The First Circuit's decision on the government's stay motion will be the next critical milestone.

Legal Landscape

The Massachusetts case is one of at least three active lawsuits challenging the fee, with two others pending in the D.C. Circuit and the Northern District of California. Judge Sorokin's ruling drew on the Supreme Court's recent decision striking down presidential tariffs, establishing the principle that the president cannot unilaterally impose taxes without congressional approval.

Twenty Democratic-led states brought the Massachusetts challenge. If the First Circuit allows Judge Sorokin's ruling to go into effect, it would apply nationwide, removing the fee requirement for all qualifying H-1B petitions.

The appeal is pending as State of California, et al. v. Mullin, et al., No. 26-1699, in the First Circuit.
